On the way out, field_serializer, L224 and model_serializer, L355 attach custom dumping behavior, recorded as FieldSerializerDecoratorInfo, L92. For inline use inside Annotated, PlainSerializer, L21 and WrapSerializer, L91 wrap a function so it travels with the type annotation itself rather than with a specific class.

Once the core schema exists, the JSON Schema side is a read-only projection. GenerateJsonSchema, L223 walks the core schema and emits the standard document, and because it is a class you can subclass, teams customize titles, descriptions, or OpenAPI-flavored output without touching validation. Edge shapes are supported too: RootModel, L34 wraps a bare root value when the whole payload is, say, a list rather than an object.

This composability is exactly why the library has become the lingua franca for structured data in the LLM world. instructor leans on pydantic models to turn free-form chat completions into typed objects, and the validation errors loop straight back into the prompt as repair feedback. The pydantic team’s own pydantic-ai framework uses the same models to type agent tools and results, and the MCP Python SDK describes tool inputs and outputs with them as well. Learn one model syntax here and you have learned the interface all three expect.

Honest Limits

A few things worth knowing before you build on this tour:

  • The Python layer is not where the speed lives. The validation and serialization hot loops run inside the Rust pydantic-core crate, which this tour deliberately did not open. The Python package’s job — metaclass orchestration, schema building, decorator bookkeeping — happens once per class definition, not per instance.
  • No benchmark numbers here on purpose. The README advertises pydantic as “Fast” without publishing figures in that document, and we did not run our own measurements, so this post makes no performance claims.
  • V2 is a different library from V1. The README states plainly that Pydantic V2 is “a ground-up rewrite” with breaking changes. The repository ships an in-tree V1 compatibility copy under pydantic/v1/ (usable as from pydantic import v1 as pydantic_v1), and deprecated helpers such as parse_obj_as, L31 still live in pydantic/deprecated/. Settings management, formerly BaseSettings, moved to the separate pydantic-settings package; the in-repo pydantic/env_settings.py is explicitly a “backport module from V1” per its own docstring.
  • Line numbers drift. We toured main at version 2.15.0a0+dev. Every file and line cited here was verified with search at writing time, but main moves; the diagrams and their click-through links reflect the branch as of this post’s date.
  • Schema building has a real cost. The metaclass work is per-class, but huge models, deeply nested unions, and heavy decorator use all widen the schema-building step; deferred builds via the mock placeholders exist precisely because some classes cannot be completed eagerly.

If you want to go deeper into the ecosystem after this tour, the structured-output workflow in instructor is the natural next stop, and the agent-side patterns in pydantic-ai show the same models driving tool-calling loops end to end.
entry.summary: A guided architecture tour of the pydantic repository on main, from ModelMetaclass class construction to core schema generation, validators, serializers, and JSON Schema output.

entry.title: Ray Source Tour: How Tasks, Actors and the Object Store Fit Together

link.title: Ray Source Tour: How Tasks, Actors and the Object Store Fit Together

entry.content:
Ray began as a research project at UC Berkeley and grew into what its README now calls “a unified framework for scaling AI and Python applications.” The pitch is simple: the same Python you run on your laptop should run on a cluster with minimal changes. What makes that work is a surprisingly compact core — a driver library that decorates your functions and classes, a set of per-node processes that schedule and execute work, and a distributed object store that moves the results around. In this tour we read the actual Python source of ray-project/ray (the python/ray package on the master branch) and trace a call from ray.init() down to the C++ core worker and back.

The two diagrams below were generated from the repository itself: every node links to a real file on GitHub, and every symbol we mention is one we located with a line-number search in the working tree. The first diagram is a map of the whole system — the public API, the cluster bootstrap machinery, the task and actor paths, and the object layer. The second goes deeper into internals: function export and registration, actor creation, and how ray.put and ray.get interact with the core worker. If you have read our earlier tours of single-machine tools like Dask, this is the natural next step: Ray’s design decisions only become visible at cluster scale.

Ray overview — twelve files that define the system's shape. Click any node to open the source on GitHub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • ray.init at L1448 in _private/worker.py is the front door. It either attaches to an existing cluster or builds a local one, and the module-level global_worker = Worker() at L1408 means every process has exactly one worker instance.
  • Node at L73 in _private/node.py describes one machine’s configuration, and ray.init constructs it at L1930 for the head-node case.
  • The process launcher in _private/services.py — start_ray_process at L883, with dedicated helpers like start_gcs_server at L1523 and start_raylet at L1610 — actually forks the GCS, raylet, and dashboard processes you see in ps output.
  • ray.remote at L3804 is the decorator entry point. Its helper _make_remote at L3611 checks whether you decorated a function or a class and routes accordingly.
  • RemoteFunction at L41 in remote_function.py is the stateless-task wrapper. Setting self.remote = _remote_proxy at L183 is what gives your function its .remote() method, and calling the wrapper directly raises TypeError at L185.
  • ActorClass at L1553 is the stateful counterpart, and the ActorHandle at L2274 it returns is the proxy your code holds for the actor’s lifetime.
  • ObjectRef at L50 is a Cython class (cdef class ObjectRef(BaseID)) that wraps an object ID plus owner address — it is the future-like handle every task and method call returns.
  • SerializationContext at L145 registers the custom deserializers that make refs and actor handles cross process boundaries intact.
  • Above the core sit the libraries: Tuner at L43 for hyperparameter search and Dataset at L272 for data-parallel loading and transformation. Both are ordinary consumers of the task and actor APIs you see beneath them.

The Task Path: From Decorator to Worker

Follow the task path in the detail diagram. When you write @ray.remote on a function, _make_remote wraps it in a RemoteFunction whose options were validated at decoration time. Nothing runs yet. The first call of f.remote(...) lands in RemoteFunction._remote at L358, and this is where three important things happen.

First, the function is exported. Because the receiving worker is a different process that has never seen your code, Ray pickles the function and ships it through the FunctionActorManager.export at L219 method of function_manager.py. There is an export-once guard: _last_export_cluster_and_job is compared against the worker’s current cluster and job, so the pickle round-trip happens once per function per job rather than on every call. On the execution side, a worker that picks up the task calls fetch_and_register_remote_function at L289 to pull the pickled blob from the cluster’s key-value store and re-import it locally.

Second, arguments are flattened and serialized against the extracted function signature, using the machinery in SerializationContext. If an argument is itself an ObjectRef, Ray passes it by reference and the receiving worker resolves it; only plain values are inlined into the task spec.

Third, the prepared task is handed to the C++ side. The Python driver’s worker.core_worker is a ray._raylet.CoreWorker binding created at L2735 inside connect(). That single binding is the wall between the readable Python layer and the scheduling, ownership, and object-store logic implemented in C++ under src/ray (outside the Python package we toured here). The call returns immediately with an ObjectRef — Ray’s task submission is asynchronous by design, and your script only blocks when it asks for a result.

The Actor Path: Stateful Workers

Actors answer a different question: what if a worker should keep state between calls? ActorClass at L1553 is what @ray.remote produces for a class. Its metaclass-style __init__ at L1562 exists mostly to forbid subclassing an actor class directly, and __call__ raises if you try to instantiate it like a normal Python object — the only legal entry point is .remote().

That call goes to ActorClass._remote at L1883. It validates naming and namespace options, exports the class definition through export_actor_class at L488 in the same manager the task path uses, computes the actor’s resource footprint, and finally invokes core_worker.create_actor at L2193. The result is wrapped into an ActorHandle at L2274 — note the original_handle=True argument at creation, which matters for ownership: when the original handle goes out of scope, the actor itself can be destroyed.

Method calls are the elegant part. ActorHandle defines a __getattr__ at L2610 that returns an ActorMethod (the class lives at L848) for any attribute you touch. Calling it lands in _actor_method_call at L2486, which serializes the arguments and reaches core_worker.submit_actor_task at L2578. The return value is again one or more ObjectRefs. Concurrency semantics depend on configuration: an async actor runs tasks on an event loop, while threaded actors default to out-of-order execution — the code around L2167 shows allow_out_of_order_execution being defaulted from is_asyncio or max_concurrency > 1.

For coordination across a fixed set of actors, the standard library utility is ActorPool at L13 in util/actor_pool.py, which distributes work items over your handles and yields results as they complete. It is a small file and one of the best places to see actor handles being used the way Ray’s own authors intended.

Objects: ObjectRef, ray.put and ray.get

The object layer is the third pillar. ray.put at L3053 stores a value once and hands you a ref you can pass to any task; Worker.put_object at L810 does the work, retrying automatically when the store is full. ray.get at L2902 blocks until the value is available locally — if it lives on another node, the system ships it over first — and it will re-raise a task’s exception in your process, which is why errors from remote code look local. ray.wait at L3109 splits a list of refs into ready and not-ready without blocking on all of them, and is the standard tool for bounding how many tasks are in flight.

The ObjectRef itself, defined in Cython at includes/object_ref.pxi L50, is more than a token: it registers itself with the core worker on construction and deregisters on deallocation (L68 and the __dealloc__ that follows), which is how Ray’s distributed reference counting knows when a value can be evicted. It also supports await via as_future, so the same ref works in asyncio code. Inside a worker, get_runtime_context at L641 in runtime_context.py exposes the current job, task, and actor IDs so library code can introspect where it is running. One more detail worth knowing: in __init__.py, AUTO_INIT_APIS at L207 lists the public functions (get, put, wait, cancel, and friends) that implicitly call ray.init() for you — remote deliberately is not in that set, because decorating should never start a cluster.

Ray internals — the task path from decorator to core worker, the actor path with handles and method calls, and the object layer they both share.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything above is verifiable from the quick-start path in the README and the remote() docstring, which contains the exact example we adapt here.

Step 1 — install:

pip install ray

Step 2 — turn a plain function into a remote task with the decorator:

import ray
ray.init()

@ray.remote
def train_chunk(seed: int):
    # pretend this trains a small model and returns its score
    total = sum(i * i for i in range(seed * 1_000))
    return seed, total

Step 3 — submit all chunks at once and collect with ray.get. The calls return immediately; the loop only blocks at the single ray.get:

refs = [train_chunk.remote(s) for s in range(8)]
results = ray.get(refs)          # blocks until all eight finish
print(results[:2])

Step 4 — make it stateful. A model server is naturally an actor, and the docstring for ray.remote shows the class form verbatim:

@ray.remote
class Scorer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.calls = 0
    def score(self, x):
        self.calls += 1
        return x * 2

scorer = Scorer.remote()
ref = scorer.score.remote(21)
print(ray.get(ref))              # 42

Step 5 — scale out. The same script runs unchanged on a real cluster: start nodes with ray start --head / ray start --address=<head> and point ray.init(address=...) at the cluster. That is the whole migration story, and it is the reason the core API surface is so small — tasks, actors, and objects cover what the AI libraries need.

Where the Libraries Plug In

The overview diagram’s right edge shows two representative consumers. Ray Tune’s Tuner expresses hyperparameter search as many parallel trials, each an actor or task, and borrows the scheduling and fault-tolerance of the core rather than reimplementing it. Ray Data’s Dataset decomposes a large dataset into blocks and processes them with streaming tasks, which is the same task/actor substrate again. This layering is why Ray’s README lists its AI libraries — Data, Train, Tune, RLlib, Serve — as separate products while the runtime underneath stays shared. If you are comparing distributed-dataframe options, our Modin tour (here) covers a library that can use Ray as an execution engine, and our Dask tour (here) covers its closest architectural cousin in task-graph land.

Honest Limits

Three limitations deserve plain language. First, the C++ heart is out of scope here: scheduling policy, the ownership model described in the “Ownership” paper referenced in the README, and the Plasma-derived object store live in src/ray, so this tour stops at the CoreWorker binding — the diagrams describe the Python side truthfully, but the most interesting scheduling code is on the far side of that wall. Second, the Python package is enormous (over ten thousand files in the sparse checkout we searched), and much of its bulk is tests, autoscaler cloud providers, and protocol-generated code; the handful of files we anchor on are the ones the public API actually routes through. Third, we deliberately quote no performance numbers in this post: any claim about throughput or latency would need a benchmark we did not run, and the README itself makes no such claims. What we can say is structural — Ray trades a small, stable API for a large amount of process machinery, and reading the source makes that trade visible: ray.init starts real operating-system processes, decoration creates real wrappers with real validation, and every .remote() call crosses a language boundary. Understanding those costs is exactly what a source tour is for. For inference-scale serving built on similar distributed runtimes, see our vLLM (tour) and SGLang (tour).
entry.summary: A guided architecture tour of the ray-project/ray Python package, from ray.init to ActorHandle and ObjectRef, with clickable diagrams.

entry.title: Vanna Source Tour: Inside the Text-to-SQL Agent Framework

link.title: Vanna Source Tour: Inside the Text-to-SQL Agent Framework

entry.content:
Vanna is an open-source Python framework that turns natural-language questions into SQL queries and, ultimately, into charts and summaries. You feed it your schema (DDL), business documentation, and sample queries; it embeds and stores them, then retrieves the most relevant context at question time to prompt the LLM. The current main branch carries a major turning point: version 2.0 is a ground-up rewrite that turns the old “generate SQL and return it” library into a user-aware, streaming, tool-based agent platform.

That rewrite is exactly why the source tree is worth a tour. Most LLM wrappers keep their simplicity by refusing to grow up; Vanna instead reorganized itself into a clean layered architecture — a framework core with seven explicit extension points, a set of capability contracts, a large integrations directory, and a preserved legacy layer for 0.x users. Reading the code, you can watch a mature project execute a migration strategy in public: the old API still runs, an adapter bridges it into the new runtime, and the new design is opinionated about identity, permissions, and streaming from day one.

In this tour we walk the actual main branch of Vanna-AI/vanna, module by module, with verified file paths and line anchors. Two diagrams anchor the discussion: a compact overview of the moving parts, and a detailed map covering the extension interfaces, integrations, and the legacy subsystem. Everything below links to the real source on GitHub.

Overview of Vanna 2.0 on the main branch: the Agent orchestrates an LLM service, a tool registry, and a user resolver; integrations supply OpenAI, Anthropic, and database adapters; servers expose the chat over HTTP; and the legacy 0.x surface plugs in through an adapter.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Agent, L56 — the orchestrator. Its constructor at L82 wires an LLM service, a tool registry, a user resolver, memory, and seven optional extension points, while send_message, L141 streams UI components back to the caller.
  • DefaultWorkflowHandler, L32 — the built-in chat-turn logic. The Agent delegates each incoming message here; this implementation decides when to call tools, when to ask the LLM to summarize, and what starter UI a new conversation renders.
  • ToolRegistry, L46 — where tools live. Every capability the agent can use is registered here, with access groups checked against the resolved user.
  • Tool, L16 — the typed contract every tool implements: a name, a description, a Pydantic args schema, and an async execute that receives a ToolContext, L28 carrying the user and returns a ToolResult, L47 with a result_for_llm and an optional UI component.
  • RunSqlTool, L18 — the flagship tool. It takes any injected SqlRunner, executes the query, saves the result as a CSV artifact for downstream tools, and streams a DataFrameComponent so the frontend renders a real table.
  • LlmService, L13 — the provider seam. Concrete adapters include OpenAILlmService, L27, an OpenAIResponsesService, L14 variant on the newer Responses API, and AnthropicLlmService, L27.
  • register_chat_routes, L17 — the delivery seam. A ChatHandler, L12 binds the agent to HTTP routes, exposing an SSE streaming chat endpoint that the prebuilt <vanna-chat> web component consumes.
  • VannaBase, L72 — the old world, kept alive under src/vanna/legacy/. The classic ask / train / generate_sql surface still works there, and LegacyVannaAdapter, L66 wraps an existing 0.x instance so it can serve as the tool registry and memory of a 2.0 agent.

The detailed map: the agent core exposes pluggable interfaces for prompts, storage, caching middleware, hooks, context enrichment, and observability; capability contracts define what a tool, a memory, or a database runner must look like; integrations fill those contracts with real providers; and the legacy layer preserves the 0.x API.

What Vanna Is and Why It Changed

The 0.x design was famously simple: you mixed a vector-store class with an LLM class and got an object that could train() and ask(). Behind the scenes, DDL statements, documentation, and question-SQL pairs were embedded and stored, and at question time the most similar items were retrieved and injected into the prompt. That design made text-to-SQL accessible to anyone who could write two lines of Python.

But production deployments need things a class mixin cannot express cleanly: who is asking, which rows they may see, how results stream to a browser, and how to audit every query. Vanna 2.0 answers those questions structurally. The README’s own summary of the rewrite names the shift: agent-based instead of VannaBase class methods, user-aware at every layer, streaming rich UI components instead of text and dataframes, and web-first with a bundled <vanna-chat> component and server. The MIGRATION_GUIDE.md at the repo root documents the break and offers a genuinely incremental path: wrap your old vn object, ship the new UI, then migrate tool by tool.

The Agent Core: One Orchestrator, Seven Hooks

src/vanna/core/ is the framework’s heart, and its design rewards a close read. The Agent class itself is surprisingly thin — it mostly stores dependencies and defaults. When no conversation store is passed, it imports and instantiates a MemoryConversationStore automatically; when no context enhancer is given, it builds a DefaultLlmContextEnhancer from the agent memory.

The seven documented extension points are each a single abstract base class in its own subpackage: LlmMiddleware, L15 intercepts LLM requests and responses for caching or cost tracking; LifecycleHook, L17 fires at message and tool-execution boundaries for quota checks and logging; ToolContextEnricher, L15 adds data to tool context; LlmContextEnhancer, L16 folds retrieved memories into prompts; ConversationStore, L14 persists history; ObservabilityProvider, L14 collects traces and metrics; and SystemPromptBuilder, L15 shapes the system prompt. Configuration lives in AgentConfig, L113, covering streaming, temperature, UI feature flags, and audit settings. The default workflow handler actually consumes all of it: it runs the agent loop — status updates, tool calls through the registry, streamed UI components — with each phase interceptable by a different hook. A textbook ports-and-adapters layout, applied to an LLM stack.

Tools, Users, and Row-Level Awareness

The capability contracts live in two places: src/vanna/core/tool/ for the tool protocol and src/vanna/capabilities/ for the database-facing interfaces. A tool is generic machinery — arguments, execution, results — while a capability such as SqlRunner, L18 or AgentMemory, L23 describes a need the framework has. Integrations fill those needs: SqliteRunner, L10 for SQLite, MemoryConversationStore for conversations, and ChromaAgentMemory, L42 for embedding-backed memories.

User-awareness is the headline feature, and it flows through identity first. A UserResolver, L14 extracts a User, L12 — an id, an email, and group memberships — from cookies, JWTs, or whatever your app already uses. That user object rides inside every ToolContext, tools declare which access groups they require, and the README documents the intended end state: SQL filtered per user before it ever runs. The RunSqlTool path shows the mechanics: it receives the context, calls the injected runner with it, and leaves enforcement to the runner implementation — where your database-side row-level policies plug in.

The Legacy Layer: Where 0.x Lives On

src/vanna/legacy/ is the entire 0.x codebase, relocated but not abandoned. The abstract base class VannaBase, L72 still declares the classic surface: generate_sql, L93 builds the retrieval-augmented prompt and submits it; ask, L1692 chains SQL generation, execution, and Plotly visualization into one call; train, L1807 accepts DDL, documentation, question-SQL pairs, or a full plan; and the retrieval primitives — get_similar_question_sql, L407, get_related_ddl, L420, get_related_documentation, L433 — define what any vector store must provide. Storage training data flows through add_question_sql, L446, and generate_questions, L356 mines stored pairs for suggested follow-ups.

Two mixes complete the classic stack. ChromaDB_VectorStore, L15 implements the storage side — its add_question_sql, L67 persists a question-SQL pair and its get_similar_question_sql, L237 retrieves neighbors at query time. OpenAI_Chat, L8 implements the prompt side, with a system_message, L44 hook and a submit_prompt, L53 that token-counts and calls the client. Training payloads are shaped by dataclasses in legacy/types/__init__.py — notably TrainingPlanItem, L215 and TrainingPlan, L234 — and the old Flask UI survives as VannaFlaskApp, L1208, with deterministic content-hash ids from deterministic_uuid, L51.

Vector-store choices matter: we have covered Chroma and pgvector in earlier tours, and Vanna’s legacy tree ships connectors for both alongside Marqo, Qdrant, Weaviate, FAISS, and Pinecone.

From Install to Your First Model

The classic flow from the README needs nothing more than pip and an API key:

pip install vanna

Then build an instance by mixing a vector store with an LLM. In the current tree these classes live under the legacy subpackage, so the imports below use those paths:

from vanna.legacy.chromadb.chromadb_vector import ChromaDB_VectorStore
from vanna.legacy.openai.openai_chat import OpenAI_Chat

class MyVanna(ChromaDB_VectorStore, OpenAI_Chat):
    def __init__(self, config=None):
        ChromaDB_VectorStore.__init__(self, config=config)
        OpenAI_Chat.__init__(self, config=config)

vn = MyVanna(config={'api_key': 'sk-...', 'model': 'gpt-4o'})

Next, teach it your schema. The README’s training section shows three kinds of knowledge — DDL statements, business documentation, and sample SQL queries that demonstrate the dialect and conventions you expect back:

vn.train(ddl="CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), age INT)")
vn.train(documentation="Our business defines XYZ as ...")
vn.train(sql="SELECT name, age FROM customers WHERE name = 'John Doe'")

Finally, connect a database (or set vn.run_sql yourself) and ask a question in plain English — the README’s example is vn.ask("What are the top 10 customers by sales?") — and you get the generated SQL, a results table, and a Plotly chart in one call.

The 2.0 flow trades the mixin for composition, per the README’s production example: create an AnthropicLlmService or OpenAILlmService, register a RunSqlTool over a SqliteRunner (or another database runner), subclass UserResolver to plug in your auth, construct the Agent, and hand a ChatHandler to register_chat_routes on your existing FastAPI app. The frontend is then a single <vanna-chat> tag pointed at the SSE endpoint. If you already have a 0.x instance trained and running, the migration guide’s quick path is to wrap it with LegacyVannaAdapter and serve it through the new agent runtime — no retraining required. The agent core is framework-agnostic, so it also pairs naturally with the ecosystems in our LangChain and FastChat tours.

Honest Limits

The rewrite is real, and so is the disruption. Here is what the source and docs actually say:

  • The legacy import paths have drifted. README_LEGACY.md still shows from vanna.openai.openai_chat import OpenAI_Chat, but in the current tree those modules live under src/vanna/legacy/, and the migration guide itself imports from vanna.legacy.adapter import LegacyVannaAdapter. Follow the migration guide’s paths, not the legacy README’s, if you are on a recent build.
  • Defaults are in-memory. When you construct an Agent without a conversation store, you get MemoryConversationStore — perfect for development, gone on restart. Production deployments need to inject a real ConversationStore.
  • Row-level security is a pattern, not a switch. Identity and groups flow to every tool, but the actual SQL filtering is your job inside a SqlRunner implementation. The README describes the mechanism; your policy is your code.
  • No independent benchmarks. The repo’s own materials (README, migration guide, papers directory) describe capability, not measured accuracy. Text-to-SQL accuracy depends heavily on your DDL quality, documentation, and example queries — evaluate on your own schema.
  • 0.x code is maintained, not developed. Everything under src/vanna/legacy/ exists to keep existing users running and to feed the adapter. New capabilities land in the agent core.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the Vanna-AI/vanna codebase: agent core, tool registry, LLM and vector-store integrations, and the legacy 0.x layer, with a full architecture map.

entry.title: Guidance Source Tour: The Architecture Behind Constrained LLM Generation

link.title: Guidance Source Tour: The Architecture Behind Constrained LLM Generation

entry.content:
Most libraries that talk to language models treat the model as an oracle: you send a prompt, you get text back, and you pray it parses. Guidance — the open-source project maintained under the guidance-ai organization and originally developed at Microsoft — takes the opposite stance. Its README calls it “an efficient programming paradigm for steering language models”: you write ordinary Python, interleave prompts and generation with system(), user(), and assistant() blocks, and constrain the model’s output with regular expressions and context-free grammars. Output that must match a schema matches that schema by construction, not by hope.

What makes Guidance worth a source tour rather than just an API summary is that the constraint machinery is not a thin wrapper. When you write gen(name="expr", regex=r"\d+([+*]\d+)*"), that string travels through a grammar-builder layer, gets serialized into an AST of node objects, is interpreted node by node against an abstract Interpreter protocol, and finally lands in an Engine that constrains logits at the token level — fast-forwarding tokens the grammar already determines.

This post walks that whole path in the current code (version 0.3.2 on the main branch). We generated two clickable architecture diagrams directly from the repository: an overview with the twelve components that matter, and a detail diagram with thirty components and forty-four relationships covering the library functions, the parsing layer, the engine internals, and the trace-and-widget subsystem. Every class and line number below was verified against the actual tree.

Overview of the guidance repository: from the package surface on the left, through grammar builders and the node AST, to the Model object and the engine-backed backends on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The package entry point guidance/__init__.py, L23 does something unusual: it swaps the module’s own class so that import guidance gives you a callable module — calling it applies the decorator.
  • That decorator lives in _guidance.py, L17 as def guidance(...), with GuidanceFunction at L44 binding the Model argument into wrapped functions.
  • The everyday surface — gen() at L13, select(), capture(), and the role context managers starting at role() L8 in _role.py — is aggregated by the library package.
  • Grammar builders in _grammar.py, L27 produce the node tree defined in _ast.py at GrammarNode L208.
  • A byte-level parser, ByteParser at L197, validates strings against those grammars offline — no API calls needed.
  • Everything flows through the immutable Model class at L58, whose __add__ at L100 copies state on every lm += ....
  • Model copies drive an Interpreter at L32, which hands nodes to the token-level Engine at L38.
  • Concrete backends — Transformers, LlamaCpp, OpenAI, Mock — are exported from models/__init__.py, L10.

The Grammar Layer: Everything Is a Node

The foundation is guidance/_grammar.py, a module of pure builder functions: string() at L19, regex() at L23, gen() at L27, select() at L61, repeat() at L117, token_limit() at L141, with_temperature() at L156, capture() at L175, and subgrammar() at L182 for embedding a separately compiled grammar. None of these touch a model. They return node objects.

Those nodes live in guidance/_ast.py, and the hierarchy is worth reading top to bottom. ASTNode at L150 is the abstract base; GrammarNode at L208 adds the operations that let nodes compose with + and % arithmetic. The leaves are LiteralNode at L317, RegexNode at L361, SelectNode at L369 for choices, JoinNode at L397 for concatenation, RepeatNode at L420, and RuleNode at L464 for named rules. Two special subclasses — SubgrammarNode at L544 and JsonNode at L568 — carry precompiled grammars and JSON Schema definitions respectively. The same file also defines Function at L99, the wrapper that makes a @guidance-decorated function composable inside expressions, plus the RoleStart and RoleEnd chat-turn markers.

Compared with other structured-output tools: Outlines builds finite-state machines from regexes, Instructor validates after the fact with Pydantic retries, while Guidance represents the constraint itself as a first-class serializable grammar the execution engine can reason about byte by byte. The guidance/_parser.py module proves the point: TokenParser at L27 and ByteParser at L197 let you call grammar.match("expr=12+7*3") and get a parse result back with no model involved at all — a useful debugging loop for gnarly regexes.

The Model Object: Immutability by Copying

guidance/models/_base/_model.py defines the object every backend inherits from. Model at L58 holds an interpreter, sampling parameters, and a set of trace nodes; the constructor lazily requests a renderer from the registry when echo=True, so the Jupyter widget can attach early.

The heart is __add__ at L100, and its first line is the whole philosophy: self = self.copy(). Every lm += ... returns a new Model. The README is explicit about this — “Model objects are immutable, so this is a copy” — which lets you fork a conversation and run several continuations without losing the originals. After copying, __add__ applies any active role blocks and then dispatches: a plain str is parsed into nodes, a Function is invoked with the model as argument, and an ASTNode goes to _apply_node.

_apply_node at L115 does two things per node: it records trace input — RoleStart, RoleEnd, LiteralNode, image and audio inputs each get their own attribute — then it iterates self._interpreter.run(node, ...) and records each output attribute, pushing a model-state copy onto context-local event queues as it goes. That push is what makes streaming and the live widget possible without special-casing in user code.

Reading results back is deliberately boring: __getitem__ at L223 returns whatever gen(name=...) or capture() stored, __str__ at L212 renders the full transcript including the model’s response, and stream() at L157 hands you a ModelStream at L330 that delays all execution until you iterate it.

The Engine Layer: Constrained Decoding

The Model never talks to weights or APIs itself. Underneath sits the engine subsystem: Engine at L38 is the abstract engine owning a tokenizer pair, EngineInterpreter at L16 translates each GrammarNode into engine calls, EngineState at L7 tracks which bytes have been committed so parsing resumes correctly across state copies, and Tokenizer at L26 keeps the byte-to-token mapping symmetric.

This is where token fast-forwarding happens. Because the grammar often forces the next bytes — after <h1> there is nothing legal but </ before the matching tag name — the engine can consult the parser, recognize that the model has no freedom left, and insert the forced tokens directly. The README quantifies the benefit qualitatively: this “saves forward passes through the model, and hence reduces GPU usage.” The same machinery explains why the gen() docstring warns that max_tokens is “not exact when regular expression pattern constraints are present”: the engine ends generation as soon as the constraint allows.

For anyone extending the library: Interpreter at L32 is generic over its state type (Generic[S]), and raises UnsupportedNodeError at L107 when a backend cannot honor a node kind — so a remote API backend gracefully rejects grammar features it cannot enforce.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything above is one pip install guidance away — if you already have the backend for your model, there is nothing else to install. The README’s canonical first run uses a local Transformers model — for other local options see our llama.cpp walkthrough:

from guidance import system, user, assistant, gen
from guidance.models import Transformers

phi_lm = Transformers("microsoft/Phi-4-mini-instruct")
lm = phi_lm  # Model objects are immutable, so this is a copy

with system():
    lm += "You are a helpful assistant"

with user():
    lm += "Hello. What is your name?"

with assistant():
    lm += gen(max_tokens=20)

print(lm)

The roles come from guidance/library/_role.py — system() at L16, user() at L32, assistant() at L48 — each a context manager that pushes opener and closer blocks built on the Block class at L8, all rendered through whatever chat template the model uses.

Constrained generation is the same shape with one extra argument. To force a number: lm += gen("lm_age", regex=r"\d+", temperature=0.8). To force a multiple-choice answer: lm += select(["A", "B", "C", "D"], name="model_selection"). To force schema-valid JSON, pass a Pydantic model to the json() function at L13:

from guidance import json as gen_json

with assistant():
    lm += gen_json(name="bp", schema=BloodPressure)

loaded = json.loads(lm["bp"])

Repetition helpers like one_or_more() at L22 and zero_or_more() at L27 let you build list- and document-shaped grammars, and the README’s HTML-page example composes stateless @guidance functions into a full context-free grammar — head, body, headings, paragraphs — where closing tags are fast-forwarded automatically.

Backends, Testing, and the Jupyter Widget

The backend set exported at models/__init__.py, L10 covers the practical spectrum. Transformers at L581 wraps TransformersEngine at L345 for local Hugging Face models (more in our Transformers guide); LlamaCpp at L239 drives GGUF models through LlamaCppEngine at L78; OpenAI at L34 pairs the API client with OpenAIInterpreter at L15, which maps grammar rules onto the endpoint’s structured-output features; and two factory functions — create_azure_openai_model at L76 and create_azure_aifoundry_model at L220 — handle Azure deployments.

For development, Mock at L165 is the sleeper hit. Backed by MockEngine at L66 and a ByteTrie at L192, it replays canned bytes through the full grammar machinery — so Mock(b"<s>expr=12+7*3") followed by lm += grammar prints 12+7*3 from lm["expr"] with zero network calls. Combine that with grammar.match() and constraint logic becomes unit-testable in CI like any other pure function.

Finally, the echo path is a small real-time system of its own. The registry in guidance/registry/_registry.py hands out context-scoped singletons: get_trace_handler at L61 and get_renderer at L71. Every input and output attribute is recorded into a TraceNode at L242 tree managed by TraceHandler at L332, published as messages over TopicExchange at L16, and consumed by renderers — the base Renderer at L68, the rich JupyterWidgetRenderer at L276, and AutoRenderer at L586.

The detail diagram: seven subsystems, thirty components, forty-four verified relationships.

Honest Limits

The README is refreshingly restrained; so are we:

  • Full grammar support is backend-dependent. The README states the constraint system “can ensure that the output conforms to any context free grammar (so long as the backend LLM has full support for Guidance)”. Remote API endpoints enforce only what their structured-output features allow, and node kinds a backend cannot honor surface as UnsupportedNodeError.
  • max_tokens is approximate under regex constraints. The gen() docstring says this outright: the limit “is not exact when regular expression pattern constraints are present,” though the engine attempts to end generation as soon as the constraint is satisfied.
  • Regex matches may overshoot. For variable-length expressions the model “is free to continue the expression after a complete match,” terminating only when something off-pattern is generated — the docstring notes the ending behavior may change as the project matures.
  • Some integrations are explicitly unmaintained. The repository keeps models/broken_models/ for Anthropic, Cohere, Gemini, LiteLLM, Together, Vertex AI and friends — present in the tree, but not part of the supported __all__ export list.
  • Fast-forwarding benefits are qualitative here. The README illustrates token fast-forwarding with local-model widget examples; we did not run latency or GPU benchmarks for this post and report none.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of the guidance library: grammar nodes, the immutable Model object, engine interpreters, and the backends that make constrained decoding real.
